title: Yglesias: Trump's H-1B Fee Plan Shrinks Skilled Immigration, Not Fixes It
excerpt: In Slow Boring, Matt Yglesias argues the administration's six-figure H-1B fee, wage-weighted lottery, and OPT crackdown would dismantle — not reform — a skilled immigration system he says is already good for the economy.
body:
• In an essay titled "Trump's terrible plan to break skilled immigration," Slow Boring's Matt Yglesias argues the administration is shrinking America's skilled immigration programs under the guise of reform — through a $100,000 H-1B fee, a wage-weighted lottery, and a push to end work authorization for foreign graduates of U.S. universities.
  • Yglesias contends the existing H-1B program, though flawed, is economically beneficial: the median H-1B worker earns $130,075 a year, in the 91st percentile nationally, and research shows such workers make a net fiscal contribution 2.6 times the typical American household's.
  • He warns that killing Optional Practical Training would collapse the pipeline American companies use to hire foreign-born U.S. graduates — perversely leaving the H-1B program even more dominated by outsourcing firms.
  • His proposed fix: double or triple the number of H-1B visas and allocate them by salary rather than lottery, plus a standards-based pathway for foreign graduates of U.S. colleges to stay and work.

In an essay in his Slow Boring newsletter titled "Trump's terrible plan to break skilled immigration," Matt Yglesias argues the administration is not reforming the H-1B system but shrinking it dramatically, "under the guise of addressing legitimate concerns about them." The critique targets three pillars: a six-figure fee on H-1B visas, a shift to a wage-weighted lottery, and a plan to impose a similar $100,000 fee on foreign students working through Optional Practical Training — a move, Yglesias writes, that would "basically kill the OPT program entirely."

The case for a flawed-but-good program

Yglesias acknowledges the program's real problems: a large fraction of H-1B recipients, he writes, are U.S.-based staff of companies "whose main line of work is outsourcing I.T. work, usually to India." But he argues the backlash has gone too far. Citing research by Adam Ozimek and Sarah Eckhardt, he notes the median H-1B worker earns $130,075 per year — the 91st percentile nationally — and that the average H-1B household makes a net federal fiscal contribution 2.6 times the typical American household's: "a big win for the federal budget." Even setting aside research on innovation spillovers, he writes, "it's just straightforwardly a good thing to have these high-earning workers in the country."

"If you took the program exactly as it existed pre-Trump, made zero reforms, fixed zero problems, and just made it bigger, that would be good."

— Matt Yglesias, Slow Boring

Why the fee plan breaks more than it fixes

The administration's centerpiece — first a proclamation, now proposed regulations after a court struck the proclamation down as an unconstitutional tax — would add $100,000 to an H-1B hire from abroad. Yglesias concedes the theoretical virtue: a six-figure fee would price out the cheapest, most exploitative uses. "But think about the numbers here," he writes: the median H-1B worker earns $130,075, and a $100,000 fee "kills off not just the bottom 20-30 percent of current H-1B uses — it kills off the *typical* H-1B job." Extending the fee to OPT compounds the damage: taxing a company $100,000 to hire a foreign-born graduate for a first job effectively ends the post-graduation pipeline — and perversely, citing an August brief by Sam Peak and Jiaxin He, collapses the student-to-OPT-to-H-1B route American companies rely on, leaving "a visa program for outsourcing companies," the very firms the crackdown was supposedly aimed at.

The wage-weighted lottery fares no better. Weighting by "Wage Level" — pay relative to occupation and labor market, not the U.S. wage distribution — produces absurdities, he writes: "an accountant in Birmingham, Ala., earning $85,000 would be at Wage Level Three. By contrast, a chemical engineer in Atlanta earning $95,000 would be at Wage Level Two." "$95,000 > $85,000. If you're talking about fiscal contribution, it's the actual salary that counts."

"It's just squeezing the balloon from multiple directions simultaneously."

— Matt Yglesias, on the combined effect of the fees and the OPT crackdown

What Yglesias would do instead

Yglesias closes with a prescription — and Trump's own 2015 rhetoric: foreign students at American colleges "should not be thrown out of our country." But 2026 is more complicated, he warns: an automatic student-to-visa pipeline invites "diploma mills as loopholes," citing Britain's experience. Instead: guardrails based on academic caliber or salary, then welcome, not exile. Recent graduates who clear those bars should get a year or two to work and prove themselves. And for H-1Bs: "Just allocate the visas preferentially to jobs that pay more." His full prescription: double or triple the number of H-1B visas and award them by salary, not lottery — "good for growth, good for the fiscal balance, and ultimately good for America."

Why this matters for the diaspora

Indian nationals receive well over half of all H-1B visas, so the fee proposals, the OPT assault (the route most Indian students use to enter the U.S. workforce), and the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period form, in Yglesias's account, an existential squeeze on the legal path Indian talent has relied on for three decades.
image_caption: Commentator Matt Yglesias. He argues that Trump's proposed H-1B fee plan would shrink skilled immigration rather than fix the system.
nri_angle: Indian nationals receive the majority of H-1B visas, so the fee proposals and the OPT crackdown Yglesias criticizes would fall hardest on Indian engineers, students, and their families.
